questions.q: A woman planning pregnancy asks about folic acid. According to current guidelines, what is the standard daily recommendation for women of childbearing age with no special risk factors?
options: No supplement needed if diet is good
questions.explanation: WHO, NICE and most national guidelines recommend 400 mcg (0.4 mg) folic acid daily, starting at least one month before conception and continuing through the first trimester, to reduce neural-tube defects. Higher doses (5 mg) are reserved for high-risk women.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks with a pre-pregnancy BMI of 22 asks how much total weight she should gain. What is the recommended range?
questions.explanation: Institute of Medicine / current guidelines recommend 11.5–16 kg (25–35 lb) total weight gain for women with normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5–24.9).

questions.q: A breastfeeding mother of a 2-month-old asks about extra energy needs. What is the approximate additional daily calorie requirement during exclusive breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: Most guidelines advise approximately 330–500 extra kcal per day during exclusive breastfeeding to support milk production and maternal recovery, depending on activity level and milk volume.

questions.q: A midwife is counselling a mother about complementary feeding. At what age does WHO currently recommend introducing complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, followed by continued breastfeeding with safe, nutrient-dense complementary foods from 6 months of age.

questions.q: A pregnant woman is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 9.5 g/dL). What is the recommended daily elemental iron intake during pregnancy according to current standards?
questions.explanation: The recommended dietary allowance / standard supplementation target for iron in pregnancy is 27 mg elemental iron daily to meet the increased requirements of expanded blood volume and fetal stores.

questions.q: Which food should a pregnant woman be advised to avoid because of the risk of Listeria?
options: Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk
questions.explanation: Soft cheeses made from unpasteurized milk, deli meats (unless reheated), and other unpasteurized dairy products carry a risk of Listeria monocytogenes, which can cause severe fetal infection.

questions.q: A preterm infant is receiving expressed breast milk. What is the current recommendation regarding vitamin D supplementation for breastfed infants?
options: Only if the mother is deficient
One single high dose at birth is sufficient
questions.explanation: Most guidelines (including NICE and AAP-aligned recommendations) advise daily vitamin D supplementation of approximately 400 IU (10 mcg) for breastfed infants because breast milk alone often provides insufficient amounts.

questions.q: A woman with gestational diabetes is learning about carbohydrate distribution. What is a key principle of medical nutrition therapy in GDM?
options: Distribute carbohydrates evenly across meals and snacks and choose high-fibre sources
questions.explanation: Current GDM nutrition guidance emphasises consistent carbohydrate distribution throughout the day, preference for complex/high-fibre carbohydrates, and monitoring of blood-glucose response rather than total carbohydrate elimination.

questions.q: During the first 6 months of exclusive breastfeeding, what is the recommended advice regarding additional water or other fluids for a healthy term infant in a temperate climate?
options: Offer water several times a day
questions.explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding meets all fluid requirements of a healthy term infant in the first 6 months; additional water or other fluids are unnecessary and may interfere with milk intake.

questions.q: A postnatal mother asks when she can safely resume a low-calorie weight-loss diet. What is the most appropriate advice while she is exclusively breastfeeding?
options: Gradual weight loss is acceptable after milk supply is established; avoid severe restriction
Wait until complete weaning before any calorie reduction
questions.explanation: Modest, gradual weight loss (approximately 0.5 kg per week) is generally considered safe once breastfeeding is well established, provided nutrient intake remains adequate. Severe calorie restriction can reduce milk supply.
